ety.text: From Middle English to, from Old English tō, from Proto-Germanic *tō ~ *ta, from Proto-Indo-European *de ~ *do (“to”). Cognate with Scots tae, to (“to”), North Frisian to, tö, tu (“to”), Saterland Frisian tou (“to”), Low German to (“to”), Dutch toe, te (“to”), German zu (“to”), West Frisian ta (“to”). Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian ndaj (“towards”), Irish do (“to, for”), Breton da (“to, for”), Welsh i (“to, for”), Russian до (do, “to”). Doublet of too.
Borrowed from Hindi तो (to).

senses.d: A particle used for marking the following verb as an infinitive.
ex: I want to leave.
He asked me what to do.

senses.d: As above, with the verb implied.
ex: "Did you visit the museum?" "I wanted to, but it was closed."
If he hasn't read it yet, he ought to.

senses.d: Used to indicate an obligation on the part of, or a directive given to, the subject.
ex: You are to go to the store and buy a bottle of milk.
I went to the shops to buy some bread.
She looked to the heavens.

senses.d: Indicating destination or final position: In the direction of, so as to arrive at or reach.
ex: We are walking to the shop.
The water came right to the top of this wall.

senses.d: Used to indicate the target or recipient of an action.
ex: I gave the book to him.
I spoke to him earlier.

senses.d: So as to contact, press against, impact, etc.
ex: I fixed the notice to the wall.
Put your shoulder to the door.

senses.d: So as to become or reach: indicating a terminal state resulting from an action.
ex: His face was beaten to a pulp.
I sang my baby to sleep.

senses.d: So as to bring about or elicit (an effect or outcome).
ex: He made several bad-taste jokes to groans from the audience.
I tried complaining, but it was to no effect.

senses.d: Used after an adjective to indicate its application.
ex: similar to ..., relevant to ..., pertinent to ..., I was nice to him, he was cruel to her, I am used to walking.

senses.d: Indicating a degree or level reached.
ex: It was to a large extent true.
We manufacture these parts to a very high tolerance.

senses.d: Used to describe what something consists of or contains.
ex: Anyone could do this job; there's nothing to it.
There's a lot of sense to what he says.

senses.d: Denotes the end of a range.
ex: It takes 2 to 4 weeks to process typical applications.

senses.d: Toward a closed, touching, or engaging position.
ex: Please push the door to.
He went in his room, pushed the door to, without fastening the latch.

senses.d: A filler word common amongst urban Indians.
ex: I am to so bored right now.

ety.text: From Middle French en, from Old French en, from Latin in, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).
Inherited from Latin in.

According to Coromines and Pascual, from Old Spanish fazia (attested ca. 1300), with the variant faza (att. in Cid, Berceo, Calila e Dimna), and in pre-literary Latinized spelling faze ad (att. 1208, in a legal document), from Latin faciem ad (facing towards).
Inherited from Middle French contre, from Old French contre, from Latin contra.
By surface analysis, univerbation of en + vers; cognate with Italian inverso.
